messages.subject: Sub-global models using AICcmodavg
parts:
Hello everyone,
I am fairly new to R and still learning so I apologize if this is a silly question. I am using unmarked to run occupancy models for jaguar and puma. I want to obtain c-hat of a global model using mb.gof.test in AICcmodavg. I have 17 possible covariates and when I include all these in the global model I get the error message "error in evaluating the argument 'object' in selecting a method for function 'summary': Error: Hessian is singular.  Try providing starting values or using fewer covariates." 

I am not sure if there is a way around this, except that I understand I should then create sub-global models; however, my question is how do I determine which variables to include in each sub-global model? Am I right in assuming then that after I compute c-hat for each sub-global model I am to choose the smallest one? 

Thank you very much,
Holly

messages.author: 58a62321f08f30f8
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Sub-global models using AICcmodavg
parts:
Hi Holly,

 

Depending on the size of the data set (e.g., number of sites), it might be the case that the global model is simply over parameterized. If you think about it in terms of ‘unique’ covariate combinations, if you have as many as you do sites for example, this could result in ‘singularity’. If you could a little more info about the data that might help diagnose the problem.

 

You could also check those covariates for collinearity (correlations among the predictors) and remove covariates based on high correlations – usually you would keep the ones that are of more interest to you.

 

Regarding sub-models, I don’t have a suggestion for that, but if you are able to remove correlated covariates that might get you a ‘subset’.

 

Chris

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Sub-global models using AICcmodavg
parts:
Hi Chris, 
Thank you very much for your response. I think you are exactly right and it is over parameterized. There are so many covariates because I created variables that were both categorical and ordinal. For example for brocket deer, I created a prey density index based on detection histories and included this as an ordinal and a categorical variable. I have 3 other main prey species, plus large sized species combined, medium prey species combined, and all prey combined. Also an additional 3 habitat covariates. I will check for collinearity and re-evaluate. It was also suggested to me to use the actual modelled occupancy of the prey species rather than a density index, which I also think would provide a solution.  
Holly
